Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I am permanently an outsider now

vignette: Alejandro's eyes still scanned the crowded streets of Manhattan with a mix of unease and instinctual vigilance. It had been two years since his deployment to Afghanistan ended, but the memories of that fateful day lingered, refusing to be shaken off. The IED blast that killed three of his comrades was forever seared into his mind - every explosion of a car horn or revving engine triggered an immediate flashback. He would see the mangled wreckage, smell the acrid smoke, and hear the anguished cries of his friends. These vivid memories were not just painful; they also made Alejandro feel like he had no future, that everything was doomed from the start. As a financial analyst, Alejandro spent most of his days staring at spreadsheets, trying to make sense of numbers that seemed meaningless compared to the chaos he experienced during combat. But even in this sterile environment, fragments of memories would suddenly appear - a glimpse of a mangled leg, the sound of gunfire - and then vanish just as quickly. These sudden pieces made it impossible for him to piece together what really happened that day; his recollections were disjointed and unclear, leaving him with more questions than answers. What haunted Alejandro most was not just the loss he suffered but also the actions he took in its aftermath - the desperation, the fear, the anger that consumed him. He became convinced that he had acted in ways that went against who he truly was, that some fundamental part of himself had been shattered beyond repair. Alejandro's inability to reconcile his past and present selves led him to withdraw from social interactions. He stopped attending gatherings or parties, fearing that someone might ask about his experiences during the war. Talking about it would only bring up more painful memories, which he struggled to keep at bay even on good days. Open spaces also made him uneasy; he felt exposed, vulnerable, and easily targeted - as if the skyscrapers towering above him were potential snipers' nests. Avoiding these triggers became his primary coping mechanism, a way to maintain some semblance of control over his emotions. However, this avoidance only strengthened Alejandro's negative appraisals of himself. By not confronting his fears or memories head-on, he reinforced the notion that he was hopeless and forever changed - an outsider looking in at a world that seemed whole and unscathed while he felt broken and fragmented. His memories continued to torment him, each recollection fueling the cycle of self-doubt and despair. Lately, Alejandro has been waking up to nightmares more frequently, reliving the same traumatic scenes with eerie vividness. The cumulative effect is starting to seep into his daily life; he's begun to struggle at work, unable to concentrate on tasks that once came easily. It was this creeping sense of dysfunction - and a dawning realization that avoidance wasn't working - that finally brought Alejandro to seek help. He hopes that by confronting the very memories he's tried so hard to suppress, he might slowly rebuild a future worth living in, one where his past no longer defines him as an outsider forever trapped in a cycle of pain.
